questions.question:
“Government is not the solution to our problem; government is the problem. From time to time we've been tempted to believe that society has become too complex to be managed by self-rule... It is my intention to curb the size and influence of the Federal establishment...”
— President Ronald Reagan, First Inaugural Address, January 1981

The economic philosophy championed by President Reagan in his inaugural address—often called 'Reaganomics' or supply-side economics—prioritized:
options: Broad federal tax cuts, reduction of government regulatory oversight on corporations, and domestic spending cuts combined with increased military expenditures
Massive expansion of federal entitlement programs and higher corporate tax brackets
The nationalization of major commercial airlines and energy telecommunication companies
The total elimination of the U.S. military budget to achieve an immediate balanced budget
questions.explanation: Supply-side economics argued that cutting corporate and marginal income taxes (such as the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981) and slashing federal regulations would stimulate private capital investment, increase productivity, and spur economic growth, though it substantially expanded national debt due to historic defense spending increases.
questions.citation: College Board AP® U.S. History CED — Unit 9: Topic 9.2 The Reagan Revolution

questions.question: Which of the following factors contributed most directly to the dissolution of the Soviet Union in December 1991 and the formal conclusion of the Cold War?
options: Severe internal Soviet economic stagnation, the burden of the Afghan War, and Mikhail Gorbachev's reform policies of glasnost (openness) and perestroika (restructuring)
A successful NATO ground invasion of Eastern European satellite nations
The total refusal of the United States to negotiate bilateral nuclear arms treaties with Moscow
The military unification of East and West Germany under Soviet political domination
questions.explanation: The Soviet system was crippled by structural economic inefficiencies, excessive military spending, and popular unrest. General Secretary Mikhail Gorbachev introduced glasnost (political transparency) and perestroika (economic restructuring), which inadvertently unleashed nationalist independence movements across Eastern Europe and Soviet republics, culminating in the USSR's collapse in 1991.
questions.citation: College Board AP® U.S. History CED — Unit 9: Topic 9.3 The End of the Cold War

questions.question: Operation Desert Storm (1991), authorized by President George H.W. Bush under a United Nations mandate, was launched to:
options: Expel Iraqi military forces from Kuwait following Saddam Hussein's unprovoked invasion and safeguard Persian Gulf oil supplies
Overthrow the Ba'athist government in Baghdad and establish an American military occupation in Iraq
Dismantle terrorist training camps in rural eastern Afghanistan
Annex Kuwait as an overseas naval territory of the United States
questions.explanation: After Saddam Hussein invaded and annexed neighboring Kuwait in August 1990, President George H.W. Bush built a 34-nation international coalition backed by UN Security Council resolutions. Operation Desert Storm liberated Kuwait in a lightning 100-hour ground campaign while deliberately stopping short of toppling Hussein's regime.
questions.citation: College Board AP® U.S. History CED — Unit 9: Topic 9.3 The End of the Cold War

questions.question: The North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA), signed into law by President Bill Clinton in 1993, aimed to:
options: Eliminate tariffs and trade barriers between the United States, Canada, and Mexico to create a continental free-trade zone
Establish a single shared currency modeled on the European euro across North America
Prohibit American manufacturers from relocating factory operations outside U.S. borders
Impose strict protective import quotas on Mexican and Canadian agricultural goods
questions.explanation: NAFTA eliminated tariffs and trade restrictions among the US, Mexico, and Canada. Proponents argued it boosted economic efficiency and exports; critics (including labor unions) argued it accelerated the outsourcing of American manufacturing jobs to lower-wage Mexican maquiladoras.
questions.citation: College Board AP® U.S. History CED — Unit 9: Topic 9.4 A Changing Economy

questions.question: The rapid economic expansion of the late 1990s under the Clinton administration was driven primarily by:
options: The emergence of personal computing, the commercialization of the Internet and World Wide Web, and unprecedented productivity gains in telecommunications
A return to strict international mercantilist trade monopolies
Massive federal government infrastructure construction comparable to the New Deal
Unprecedented spikes in international crude oil prices
questions.explanation: The 1990s witnessed the birth of the digital 'New Economy'. Proliferation of personal computers, the Internet, e-commerce, and software innovation dramatically raised worker productivity, fueled surging tech stock markets, and contributed to federal budget surpluses from 1998 to 2001.
questions.citation: College Board AP® U.S. History CED — Unit 9: Topic 9.4 A Changing Economy

questions.subtopic: The 2000 Presidential Election & Bush v. Gore (Period 9: 1980–Present)
questions.question: In the controversial Supreme Court decision Bush v. Gore (2000), the Court halted manual recounts in Florida on the grounds that:
options: The differing recount standards used by individual Florida counties violated the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment
State courts had no constitutional authority to hear election dispute lawsuits
The Electoral College system had been superseded by popular vote majorities
Presidential elections could only be decided by the House of Representatives
questions.explanation: In a 5–4 per curiam ruling, the Supreme Court held that the absence of uniform statewide recount standards across Florida counties violated the Fourteenth Amendment's Equal Protection Clause. Because Florida's statutory recount deadline had arrived, the Court halted the recount, effectively awarding Florida's 25 electoral votes and the presidency to George W. Bush.
questions.citation: College Board AP® U.S. History CED — Unit 9: Topic 9.5 Migration and Immigration in the 1990s and 2000s

questions.question: In the immediate aftermath of the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001, the United States launched Operation Enduring Freedom in Afghanistan primarily to:
options: Overthrow the fundamentalist Taliban regime that had harbored Osama bin Laden and al-Qaeda's terrorist network
Secure Iraqi oil pipelines leading to the Persian Gulf
Enforce United Nations weapons inspections on Saddam Hussein's chemical stockpiles
Retaliate against Iranian naval incursions in the Strait of Hormuz
questions.explanation: Following 9/11, President George W. Bush demanded that Afghanistan's ruling Taliban surrender Osama bin Laden and shut down al-Qaeda training camps. When the Taliban refused, a US-led coalition launched military strikes, swiftly toppling the Taliban regime and initiating America's longest war.
questions.citation: College Board AP® U.S. History CED — Unit 9: Topic 9.5 Migration and Immigration in the 1990s and 2000s

questions.subtopic: The USA PATRIOT Act & Civil Liberties (Period 9: 1980–Present)
questions.question: The USA PATRIOT Act, passed overwhelmingly by Congress in October 2001, sparked intense national debate over the balance between national security and constitutional civil liberties primarily because it:
options: Expanded federal law enforcement and intelligence surveillance powers, including roving wiretaps, bulk record collection, and delayed-notice search warrants without traditional probable cause
Mandated the internment of foreign-born non-citizens in federal detention facilities
Suspended all federal elections during declared periods of elevated homeland security threats
Abolished the Fourth Amendment right against unreasonable searches in all circumstances
questions.explanation: While supporters argued the PATRIOT Act was essential to prevent future terrorist attacks by tearing down walls between foreign intelligence and domestic law enforcement, civil libertarians contended it undermined Fourth Amendment privacy rights and Fourth Amendment checks on government surveillance.
questions.citation: College Board AP® U.S. History CED — Unit 9: Topic 9.5 Challenges of the 21st Century

questions.question: The Bush administration's primary stated justification for launching the preemptive invasion of Iraq (Operation Iraqi Freedom) in March 2003 was:
options: The allegation that Saddam Hussein's regime possessed stockpiles of weapons of mass destruction (WMDs) and had operational links to global terrorist networks
Iraq's refusal to supply crude oil to international markets
An unprovoked Iraqi naval attack on American destroyers in the Persian Gulf
A direct military request from the United Nations General Assembly to depose Hussein
questions.explanation: The Bush administration articulated a doctrine of 'preemptive war', asserting that waiting for imminent threats was too dangerous in the post-9/11 era. Citing intelligence that Saddam Hussein possessed weapons of mass destruction (WMDs) and was seeking nuclear capability—claims that post-war inspections proved unfounded—the US and coalition allies invaded Iraq.
questions.citation: College Board AP® U.S. History CED — Unit 9: Topic 9.5 Challenges of the 21st Century

questions.question: The Great Recession of 2007–2009 was triggered primarily by which financial development?
options: The collapse of the American housing bubble fueled by subprime mortgage lending, complex mortgage-backed securities, and unregulated credit default swaps
A catastrophic hyperinflation crisis caused by the sudden abandonment of the fiat dollar
The imposition of 50% tariffs on imported electronics from Asian manufacturing hubs
The federal government's default on its national treasury bond obligations
questions.explanation: Widespread issuance of risky subprime home mortgages, securitized by Wall Street investment banks into complex debt instruments (MBS, CDOs), collapsed when housing prices fell. Major financial institutions (Lehman Brothers, Bear Stearns, AIG) faced insolvency, triggering a credit freeze and the worst economic crisis since the 1930s.
questions.citation: College Board AP® U.S. History CED — Unit 9: Topic 9.4 A Changing Economy

questions.question: The Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (ACA), signed into law by President Barack Obama in 2010, aimed to achieve near-universal health coverage primarily through:
options: An individual mandate, health insurance exchanges with federal subsidies, Medicaid expansion, and prohibiting insurers from denying coverage for pre-existing conditions
The creation of a single-payer healthcare system where the federal government directly employs all doctors and hospitals
The total elimination of private employer-sponsored health insurance plans
Abolishing Medicare and Medicaid in favor of private health savings accounts
questions.explanation: The ACA significantly reformed American healthcare by creating state health insurance marketplaces with income-based tax credits, expanding Medicaid, allowing young adults to stay on parents' plans until 26, and preventing insurers from excluding people with pre-existing conditions.
questions.citation: College Board AP® U.S. History CED — Unit 9: Topic 9.6 Society in the 21st Century

questions.question: Since the passage of the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965, the demographic composition of immigration to the United States has shifted dramatically, with the overwhelming majority of new immigrants arriving from:
options: Latin America and Asia
Northern and Western Europe
The Russian Federation and Eastern Europe
Australia and New Zealand
questions.explanation: The landmark 1965 Immigration Act abolished the discriminatory 1924 national origins quota system that favored northwestern Europe, replacing it with preferences for family reunification and skilled employment. Over the ensuing decades, millions of immigrants arrived from Latin America (especially Mexico) and Asia, transforming American demographics.
questions.citation: College Board AP® U.S. History CED — Unit 9: Topic 9.5 Migration and Immigration in the 1990s and 2000s

questions.subtopic: Thematic Synthesis: Federal Power vs. States' Rights
questions.question: Which of the following historical pairs represents a continuity in debates over federal power versus states' rights across different centuries?
options: The Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions (1798) and the South Carolina Nullification Crisis (1832–1833)
The Northwest Ordinance (1787) and the Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854)
The Monroe Doctrine (1823) and the Truman Doctrine (1947)
The Dawes Act (1887) and the Social Security Act (1935)
questions.explanation: Both the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions (challenging the Alien & Sedition Acts) and John C. Calhoun's South Carolina Exposition and Protest during the Nullification Crisis asserted the compact theory of the Constitution—arguing that sovereign states had the authority to nullify federal statutes they deemed unconstitutional.
questions.citation: College Board AP® U.S. History CED — Historical Thinking Skills: Continuity and Change Over Time

questions.question: The reform strategies of the Civil Rights Movement of the 1950s and 1960s were most philosophically and tactically similar to which earlier nineteenth-century movement?
options: The antebellum nonviolent moral suasion and direct action employed by Christian abolitionists like William Lloyd Garrison and Frederick Douglass
The violent labor insurrectionism of the Molly Maguires in Pennsylvania coal mines
The nativist political agitation of the Know-Nothing Party in the 1850s
The imperialist expansionism advocated by the Yellow Journalists in the 1890s
questions.explanation: Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. and the SCLC rooted their nonviolent civil disobedience in Christian moral teachings, mirroring the antebellum abolitionist movement's conviction that unjust, discriminatory human laws violated a higher moral law and must be peacefully resisted through public witness.
questions.citation: College Board AP® U.S. History CED — Historical Thinking Skills: Comparison

questions.question: The foreign policy posture advocated in George Washington's 1796 Farewell Address was most directly challenged and permanently abandoned by the United States during which historical development?
options: The ratification of the North Atlantic Treaty in 1949, committing the United States to a permanent peacetime military alliance in Europe (NATO)
The purchase of the Louisiana Territory from France in 1803
The declaration of the Monroe Doctrine in 1823
The passage of the Neutrality Acts of 1935–1937
questions.explanation: Washington warned the young nation against 'permanent alliances with any portion of the foreign world.' While the US maintained non-entanglement for 150 years, the creation of NATO in 1949 marked America's first peacetime military alliance, formally discarding isolationist tradition in favor of collective security.
questions.citation: College Board AP® U.S. History CED — Historical Thinking Skills: Continuity and Change Over Time

questions.question: How did the federal government's policy response to the 2008 Great Recession fundamentally differ from its initial response to the onset of the Great Depression under President Herbert Hoover in 1929–1931?
options: In 2008, the federal government and Federal Reserve deployed unprecedented emergency fiscal stimulus (ARRA) and multitrillion-dollar liquidity interventions (TARP, Quantitative Easing), whereas Hoover relied largely on voluntary cooperation and balanced budgets
In 2008, the government raised protective tariffs to record highs, mimicking the Smoot-Hawley Tariff
In 2008, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates to historic highs to crush inflation
In 2008, the federal government nationalized all American agricultural farms
questions.explanation: Herbert Hoover initially resisted direct federal relief and deficit spending, relying on voluntary private business pledges and balanced budgets. In 2008, the Federal Reserve slashed rates to zero and launched Quantitative Easing, while Congress passed the $700 billion TARP bank rescue and an $800+ billion fiscal stimulus package.
questions.citation: College Board AP® U.S. History CED — Historical Thinking Skills: Comparison

questions.question: The expansion of the franchise in the United States occurred in distinct historical waves. Which of the following correctly pairs an era with the primary group whose voting rights were constitutionally recognized?
options: Progressive Era (1920) — Women (Nineteenth Amendment)
Jacksonian Era (1828) — Enslaved African Americans
Reconstruction (1870) — Native Americans living on reservations
New Deal (1936) — Eighteen-to-twenty-year-old citizens
questions.explanation: The Nineteenth Amendment (ratified in 1920 during the Progressive Era) prohibited the denial of the right to vote on the basis of sex. Enslaved persons were emancipated and Black men franchised in Reconstruction (15th Amendment, 1870); 18-to-20-year-olds gained voting rights during the Vietnam War era (26th Amendment, 1971).
questions.citation: College Board AP® U.S. History CED — Historical Thinking Skills: Chronological Reasoning

questions.question: The Wagner Act (National Labor Relations Act of 1935) altered the legal standing of American labor unions in contrast to the late nineteenth century Gilded Age primarily by:
options: Legally guaranteeing workers the right to join unions and engage in collective bargaining, while prohibiting employer unfair labor practices and establishing the NLRB
Outlawing union strikes in all essential transportation and mining industries
Repealing the Sherman Antitrust Act's application to corporate monopolies
Requiring all industrial factory workers to join the American Federation of Labor
questions.explanation: In the Gilded Age, the federal government repeatedly intervened with troops and court injunctions (Pullman Strike 1894) to crush strikes. The New Deal's Wagner Act of 1935 put the power of the federal government behind workers, protecting the right to organize and bargain collectively through the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB).
questions.citation: College Board AP® U.S. History CED — Historical Thinking Skills: Causation & Continuity

questions.question: The conservationist philosophy of President Theodore Roosevelt and Gifford Pinchot in the early 1900s differed from preservationists like John Muir primarily because Roosevelt and Pinchot advocated for:
options: The scientific management and sustainable commercial utilization of public natural resources ('wise use'), rather than the complete, untouched preservation of wilderness
The immediate sale of all national forest lands to private timber corporations
The total prohibition of all human entry and recreational tourism in national parks
The transfer of all federal lands to individual state jurisdiction
questions.explanation: Roosevelt and his Chief Forester Gifford Pinchot were conservationists who believed public lands should be scientifically managed for long-term sustainable multi-use (timber, water, grazing). Preservationists like John Muir (founder of the Sierra Club) argued for leaving wilderness pristine and untouched by commercial development.
questions.citation: College Board AP® U.S. History CED — Unit 7: Topic 7.4 The Progressives

questions.question: The jurisprudence of the Warren Court (1953–1969) was characterized primarily by which judicial philosophy?
options: Judicial activism aimed at expanding civil rights, individual liberties, and protections for criminal defendants (e.g., Gideon v. Wainwright, Miranda v. Arizona, Loving v. Virginia)
Strict originalism that limited the application of the Bill of Rights to the federal government alone
Consistently striking down congressional regulations of interstate commerce as unconstitutional
Deference to state supreme courts on all constitutional questions regarding racial segregation
questions.explanation: Under Chief Justice Earl Warren, the Supreme Court issued a flurry of landmark liberal decisions that desegregated public schools (Brown), established rights for criminal defendants (Gideon, Miranda, Mapp), outlawed state bans on interracial marriage (Loving), and established the right to privacy (Griswold).
questions.citation: College Board AP® U.S. History CED — Historical Thinking Skills: Contextualization & Synthesis
